solutions.check: 26 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Time to piss, precious

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
a wee is a urination, a politer word for a piss

explanation.surface: Someone announces it is time to relieve themselves, then adds a pet name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Precious' reads as a term of endearment tacked on the end; it is really an adjective meaning affectedly dainty.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe something excessively quaint, cute or affected in manner or taste.

clue.text: Perhaps Rishi Sunak's first overturning of A&E is overlooked by Liverpool

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the letters might be arranged some other way
'first' asks for only the opening letter of the word it follows
to overturn something is to flip it, so the letters run the opposite way

blocks.note: the prime minister's first name, taken letter for letter
opening letter of the surname
the hospital department's letters, without the ampersand

explanation.surface: A satirical jab: the prime minister turning over accident-and-emergency departments, with Liverpool ignoring it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overlooked' suggests being ignored, but here it means looked out over, as a waterfront city faces the sea. A&E is Britain's Accident and Emergency hospital department.
explanation.definitionFit: Liverpool stands on the Mersey estuary facing west onto this stretch of water between Britain and Ireland.

clue.text: Almost suffer effects of excessive masturbation? That's Sprite for you!

indicators.note: 'almost' means not quite complete, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: the old schoolboy myth warns that overdoing it costs you your sight

explanation.surface: A mock-warning about self-abuse, followed by what sounds like an advert slogan for the lemonade Sprite.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on Sprite points at the soft drink; it is really a small mischievous spirit. GO BLIND loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprite is a fairy or elf, and a mischievous little creature of folklore is one kind of such spirit.

clue.text: Biden just started argument – stirred up and intimidated

indicators.note: something only just started has got no further than its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of the president's name
a row is a quarrel
eggs are beaten when stirred up vigorously

explanation.surface: The US president starts a quarrel, and the other side is riled and cowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stirred up' looks like an anagram signal but is a straight synonym, as in beating eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: To browbeat is to bully someone with stern looks and words, so the past participle matches cowed or frightened.

clue.text: Boris and Trump finally working in this way with right, to get back

indicators.note: 'finally' points at the closing letter of each preceding name

blocks.note: closing letter of the first name
closing letter of the surname
a machine that is on is working
'do it so' means do it in this way
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Johnson and Trump cooperating with the political right to stage a comeback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get back' suggests a return to power; the definition is just 'back', a verb meaning support.
explanation.definitionFit: To back a person or event is to support it with money or endorsement, which is what a patron does.

clue.text: Ignorant piece in Sun: 'A War Economy!'

indicators.note: a piece in something is a part sitting within it, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

blocks.note: runs across the headline words, from the second letter of the paper's name

explanation.surface: A dim-witted article in the Sun tabloid shouting about a war economy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' looks like a newspaper article, which fits the Sun; here it means a section of the following letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ignorant of a fact lacks knowledge of it, which is to say they have no awareness.

clue.text: New York politician and his heartless young women

indicators.note: without a heart the middle is gone and only the outside letters remain

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for the city and state
a Member of Parliament
the pronoun with its central letter removed

explanation.surface: A cruel New York politician and the young women in his orbit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' seems to describe the politician's character, but it only removes the middle letter of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: In poetry and mythology these are beautiful maidens, so the word is a literary term for girls.

clue.text: Blimey! Trump's done for, millions lost – unethical

indicators.note: when a sum is lost it goes missing, so the abbreviation for millions leaves the word
something done for is wrecked, so its letters are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like blimey
the surname taken letter for letter
M is the abbreviation for millions

explanation.surface: A gleeful headline: the former president is finished and his fortune gone because of shady dealings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Done for' looks like a verdict on the man, but it signals that his name, once shorn of the M, is jumbled. Cor and blimey are both mild British exclamations of astonishment.
explanation.definitionFit: A corrupt person is dishonest, acting for gain against moral or legal standards, which fits unethical.

clue.text: We needn't use riots as a bitter pill

definitions.note: the definition is a noun phrase; the answer is an adjective describing it

indicators.note: riots are wild disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: all eleven letters, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A protester's plea that rioting is unnecessary, however hard a thing is to swallow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riots' reads as a noun in the sentence; it signals turmoil among the letters. 'Sugaring the pill' is making bad news palatable, so a bitter pill has had no sugar.
explanation.definitionFit: A bitter pill has no sugar coating, so the answer describes it rather than naming it, playing on the idiom about sugaring the pill.

clue.text: No PM – Israel's out cold

indicators.note: 'out' here means out of order or out of place, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of these words, ten in all

explanation.surface: A political report that Israel's prime minister has been ousted and the country is left chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S is 'is', joining wordplay to definition. 'Cold' looks like weather or temperature but means emotionally distant.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold manner lacks warmth or personal feeling, so it describes someone detached and unfriendly.

clue.text: Snake might produce fart

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, to twist and turn like a road
second meaning: gas released from the bowels

explanation.surface: A schoolboy joke that a snake could break wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snake' is a verb here, pronounced to rhyme with 'find', while the flatulence sense rhymes with 'tinned'.
explanation.definitionFit: A path can twist or meander like a serpent, and breaking wind means passing intestinal gas.

clue.text: Beachwear sex initiated? Hell!

indicators.note: to be initiated is to be started off, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
Hades is the underworld of Greek myth

explanation.surface: Shocked reaction to swimwear that seems designed to get things going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initiated' reads as 'set in motion'; it asks for the first letter of the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Shades is slang for sunglasses, which people wear on the beach against the glare.

clue.text: se 14ac.
(&13dn.) Not confident, writes about the UK's current déjà-vu experience

indicators.note: 'about' suggests being turned around and moved every which way, so the letters shift

blocks.note: all eighteen letters of these three words

explanation.surface: An uncertain columnist writes about Britain living through something familiar again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writes about' looks like a journalist's topic; 'about' signals the rearrangement. The phrase opens Richard III and was applied to Britain's strike-hit winter of 1978-79.
explanation.definitionFit: Widespread strikes in 2022-23 recalled the famous late-1970s season of industrial unrest, so Britain seemed to be reliving it.

clue.text: Second head, an old lecher– just what a blundering government seeks?

definitions.text: just what a blundering government seeks?

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a head is a headland, a cape
an old goat is a lustful older man

explanation.surface: A second leader who is also a dirty old man: exactly what an incompetent administration wants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' suggests a leader, but here it is a geographical headland.
explanation.definitionFit: A government that makes mistakes looks for someone else to take the blame, and that person is the one the answer names.

clue.text: Detached, being a better bender of the truth

definitions.text: being a better bender of the truth

blocks.note: first meaning: remote, lying away from the main body

blocks.clueFragment: being a better bender of the truth
blocks.note: second meaning, split in two: surpassing someone else at telling falsehoods

explanation.surface: A cool, aloof figure who is also a superior liar.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word as OUT-LYING, like outrunning or outdoing: beating another liar at lying.
explanation.definitionFit: Remote villages or islands far from the centre are called this, and the split reading means exceeding a rival in falsehood.

clue.text: A form of service when sex is involved in unspecified disease

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be wrapped up inside it

blocks.note: 'it' is a coy word for sex
'the lurgy' is British slang for some vague, unnamed illness

explanation.surface: A dark hint that a certain sort of service comes with an infection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' suggests a sexual favour, but it is a church service. The lurgy is jokey British slang for whatever bug is going round.
explanation.definitionFit: A liturgy is the set form of public worship used in a church, a prescribed order of prayers and rites.

clue.text: Party supporter gets end away – free and very passionate

indicators.note: the end is sent away, so the final letter drops off

blocks.note: a Tory supports Britain's Conservative Party
to rid is to free, as in 'rid of'

explanation.surface: A Conservative activist has a steamy liaison, free of inhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets his end away' is British slang for having sex; here it simply cuts the final letter from TORY.
explanation.definitionFit: A torrid affair is intensely sexual and ardent, the word literally meaning scorchingly hot.

clue.text: Who abandoned the match after cover collapsed during pass?

definitions.note: a clause describing the person, standing for the noun

indicators.note: a collapsed structure falls into disorder, so these letters are rebuilt
one thing happening during another sits within its span

blocks.note: taken as written
to pass away is to die

explanation.surface: A cricket or football match called off when the pitch covers gave way during a passage of play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' looks sporting but means a marriage; the person who walked out of one is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A marriage is a match, and someone who has left or ended one legally is a formerly married person.

clue.text: Cheap and unpleasant chain meeting with Eye's abuse

indicators.note: abuse is mistreatment, and mistreated letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: CH is the abbreviation for chain, an old unit of length
the magazine's name with its possessive S

explanation.surface: A tacky high-street chain gets a roasting from Private Eye.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's magazine is Private Eye, but only the letters of its name are used. A chain is an old British measure of 22 yards.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheesy describes something tacky, of poor quality and in bad taste, cheap and a bit off-putting.

clue.text: Crummy elected president in grip of drink

indicators.note: whatever is in the grip of something is held inside it

blocks.note: a candidate who is elected is in
P is the abbreviation for president
a tot is a small measure of spirits

explanation.surface: A useless newly elected president who is a slave to the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: Tinpot usually describes a petty dictator, so the elected president is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinpot means shoddy, inferior and insignificant, just as crummy means second-rate and worthless.

clue.text: see 24dn.
All possible White House sources before getting in an untidy state?

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase, as in 'all over the place'

indicators.note: the source of a word is where it begins, so the opening letters are taken

blocks.note: every means all possible, as in 'every chance'
the initial letters of the two words
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: A newsroom mentions every source in the White House before things descend into chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sources' suggests leaks from inside the administration, but it means initial letters. Things lying everywhere are strewn all over the place.
explanation.definitionFit: A room in disorder has things scattered all over, so its contents are found in all places.

clue.text: (& 22ac.) How to effect such a strike? Use your noddle!

definitions.text: How to effect such a strike? Use your noddle!

blocks.clueFragment: How to effect such a strike?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone asks how to organise industrial action and is told to think it through
setter's reading: 'noddle' is slang for the head, so the blow is delivered with the head itself

explanation.walkthrough: 'Use your noddle' normally means use your brains; taken literally it means hit with your head. 'Strike' suggests a walkout but is a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a blow struck with the forehead, which is literally using one's noddle to hit someone.

clue.text: Suffer torment: being mature is no different inside

indicators.note: made different, the letters are arranged another way
'inside' places one set of letters within another

blocks.note: to age is to mature, grow older
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rueful observation that growing older does not change how you feel within.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No different' reads as 'unchanged', but 'different' is the signal to rearrange the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To agonise is to experience great mental anguish, especially while struggling over a decision.

clue.text: Forward – as nurses often are

definitions.note: a description split as two words, ON WARDS

blocks.note: first meaning: ahead, onward in direction
second meaning, split in two: hospital staff are stationed on hospital rooms

explanation.surface: A rallying cry, then an aside about nursing staff being pushy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forward' could mean bold, which seems to describe nurses; the second reading is where they work, split as ON WARDS.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means moving ahead in a direction, and nurses are usually stationed in hospital wards.
